# Linear First-Order Regression 

Linear regression verify the relation between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables.

In Linear regression, the factor becomes **quantitative**.

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i
$$
To establish a simple linear regression model, the following assumptions must be met:

- The relationship between $X$ and $Y$ is linear.

- The values of $X$ are fixed; in other words, $X$ is not a random variable.

- The mean of the error terms is zero: $E(\varepsilon_i) = 0$.

- For a given value of $X$, the variance of the error terms $\varepsilon_i$ is constant and equal to $\sigma^2$, representing the residual variance. This property is known as homoscedasticity.

- The error terms follow a normal distribution: $\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$.

## Example 1: Single Value

The linear model was proposed to explain the relationship between the amount of feed provided and milk production in goats. Using the data below, it is requested to verify whether feed significantly influences milk production (α = 5%).

### 1.1 Computing manually
$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\textbf{Feed level (g)} & 50 & 75 & 100 & 125 & 150 \\ \hline
\textbf{Milk production (L/day)} & 1,2 & 1,7 & 2,0 & 2,1 & 2,5 \\ 
\hline
\end{array}
$$

$$
\sum_{i=1}^5X_i=500 \quad \sum_{i=1}^5X_i^2=56.250,00 \quad \sum_{i=1}^5X_iY_i=1.025,00 
$$
$$
\sum_{i=1}^5Y_i=9,50 \quad \sum_{i=1}^5Y^2=18,99 \quad \overline{X}=100 \quad \overline{Y} = 1,90
$$

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n=n\hat{\beta_0}+\hat{\beta_1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i \\ 5\hat{\beta_0}+500\hat{\beta_1}=9,50\\
$$

$$
\sum_{i=1}^nY_iX_i=\hat{\beta_0}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i+\hat{\beta_1}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i^2\\
500\hat{\beta_0}+56.250\hat{\beta_1}=1.015\\
$$

$$
\text{Then, we divide by 100:}\\
$$

$$
\frac{500\hat{\beta_0}+56.250\hat{\beta_1}=1.015}{100} = 5\hat{\beta_0}+562,50\hat{\beta_1}=10,25 
$$
$$
5\hat{\beta_0}+500\hat{\beta_1}=9,50\\
5\hat{\beta_0}+562,50\hat{\beta_1}=10,25
$$

$$
5\hat{\beta_0}+500\hat{\beta_1}=9,50\\
\quad \quad \quad 62,5\hat{\beta_1}=0,75\\
\hat{\beta_1}
=\frac{0.75}{62.50}=0,0120\\
$$

$$
5\hat{\beta_0}+500*0,0120=9,50
\hat{\beta_0}=0.700\\
$$

$$
Then:\\
$$
$$
\hat{Y_i}=0,700+0,012X_i
$$
```{r}
x <- c(50, 75, 100, 125, 150)
y <- c(1.2, 1.7, 2.0, 2.1, 2.5)
goat <- data.frame(x, y)
goat
```
### 1.2 Scartterplot
```{r}
plot(y ~ x, pch = 19, data = goat,
     main = "Scatterplot of Milk Production vs Feed Level",
     xlab = "Feed Level (g)", ylab = "Milk Production (L/day)")
cor(goat)
```

### 1.3 Fitting the linear model

```{r}
fit1 <- lm(y ~ x)
summary(fit1)
anova(fit1)
fit1$fitted.values
fit1$res
```

### 1.4 Checking Normality test

```{r}
shapiro.test(fit1$res)
```

Final model **summary** and **statistics**

```{r}
fit2 <- lm(y ~ x)
summary(fit2)
```

So when we are working with regression, the determination coeffient is use to reffer to how much of the variation is beeing explained by the model. So the coeficient of determination is compute by:

$$
r^2=\frac{SQ_{REG}}{SQ_{Total}}100
$$

- The inclusion of numerous variables, even if they have very little explanatory power, will increase the value of $r^2$.

- The adjusted $r^2$ penalizes the inclusion of explanatory regressors that contribute very little.

So, we can compute $r_a^2$ by:

$$
r_a^2=1-\frac{n-1}{n-k}(1-r^2)
$$
**Where:**

- $n:$ is the number of observations;

- $k:$ is number of model parameters;

```{r}
R2 <- summary(fit2)$adj.r.squared; R2
anova(fit2)
coef(fit2)
confint(fit2)
```

### 1.5 Coefficiente of variation (CV)**

$$
CV = \frac{\sqrt{QM_{Ind}}}{Y}100
$$

```{r}
QMResid <- anova(fit2)[2, 3]
CV <- 100 * sqrt(QMResid) / mean(y)
CV
```

### 1.6 Plot - linear regression

```{r}
plot(y ~ x, data = goat, pch = 19, col = "red3", 
     xlim = c(48, 150), ylim = c(0.5, 3),
     xlab = "Feed Level (g)", ylab = "Milk Production (L/day)",
     main = "Feed vs Milk Production")

axis(1, xaxp = c(50, 150, 10))

# Axis break
require(plotrix)
axis.break(axis = 1, breakpos = 46, bgcol = "white", breakcol = "black",
           style = "slash", brw = 0.02)

# Add regression line
coef.m <- coef(fit2)
curve(coef.m[1] + coef.m[2] * x, 
      add = TRUE, lty = 1,
      col = "blue3", lwd = 2)

# Equation and R²
co <- format(c(coef(fit2), R2), digits = 4)
text(115, 1.45, 
     label = substitute(hat(y[i]) == b0 + b1 * x[i] ~~~~ (r^2 == r2),
     list(b0 = co[1], b1 = co[2], r2 = co[3])))

```

Ploting with confidence interval

```{r}
plot(y ~ x, data = goat, pch = 19, col = "red3", 
     xlim = c(48, 150), ylim = c(0.5, 3),
     xlab = "Feed Level (g)", ylab = "Milk Production (L/day)",
     main = "Feed vs Milk Production")

axis(1, xaxp = c(50, 150, 10))

require(plotrix)
axis.break(axis = 1, breakpos = 46, bgcol = "white", breakcol = "black",
           style = "slash", brw = 0.02)

curve(coef.m[1] + coef.m[2] * x, add = TRUE, lty = 1, col = "blue3", lwd = 2)

# Confidence intervals
xframe <- data.frame(x = seq(50, 150, by = 5))
xa <- xframe$x
ya <- predict(fit2, int = "c", newdata = xframe)

lines(xa, ya[, "lwr"], lty = 3)
lines(xa, ya[, "upr"], lty = 3)

coord <- data.frame(x = c(xa, rev(xa)), y = c(ya[, "lwr"], rev(ya[, "upr"])))
polygon(coord, border = NA, col = adjustcolor("black", alpha = 0.2))

text(115, 1.45, label = substitute(hat(y[i]) == b0 + b1 * x[i] ~~~~ (r^2 == r2),
                                   list(b0 = co[1], b1 = co[2], r2 = co[3])))
```

## Example 2: With replicates

```{r}
# Clean environment
rm(list = ls())

# Load data
setwd("C:/StatisticsCourse/11-Regression")
data <- read.table("DataSonifero.txt", header = TRUE)
head(data)
attach(data)
```

### 2.1 Assumptions checking (CRD)
```{r}
# Linear model treating x as a qualitative variable
fit1 <- lm(y ~ factor(x))
anova(fit1)

# Residuals
res <- fit1$residuals
res

# Normality test
shapiro.test(res)

# Homogeneity of variances
bartlett.test(res, x)
```

### 2.2 Scartterplot
```{r}
plot(x, y, pch = 19, col = "red", ylim = c(0, 20), main = "Scatterplot")
plot(tapply(y, x, mean) ~ unique(x), pch = 19, col = "red", ylim = c(0, 20),
     main = "Mean Response per Dose")
```

### 2.3 Fitting the model
```{r}
fit2 <- lm(y ~ x)
summary(fit2)
R2 <- summary(fit2)$r.squared; R2
anova(fit2)
coef(fit2)
confint(fit2)
```

Lack of fit and pure error
```{r}
fit3 <- lm(y ~ factor(x))
summary(fit3)
R2max <- summary(fit3)$r.squared; R2max
anova(fit3)

# Lack of fit test
anova(fit2, fit3)
```

Interpretation:

Total residual sum of squares (RSS) = 112
Pure error = 100
Lack of fit = 12 (df = 3, F = 0.4, p = 0.7561)
Not significant → model fits well

```{r}
# Real R-squared
r2real <- R2 / R2max
r2real
```

Using `expdes.pt` package

As we are working with quantitative factors, we have to set the `quali` object to `FALSE`
```{r}
library(ExpDes.pt)
dic(x, y, quali = FALSE, mcomp = "tukey", sigT = 0.05, sigF = 0.06)
```

### 2.4 Fitting polynomial regression via `reg.poly`

We first perform an ANOVA to obtain information such as degrees of freedom (DF) and sum of squares (SS) values.
```{r}
dic <- lm(y ~ factor(x))
anova(dic)
```

```{r}
reg.poly(y, x, 10, 100, 4, 132)
```

### 2.5 Regression plot and equation
```{r}
plot(y ~ x, data = data, pch = 16, col = "blue",
     xlab = "Dose of sedative (mg)", ylab = "Sleep duration (hours)",
     ylim = c(0, 20), frame = FALSE)

# Add regression line
cf.m <- coef(fit2)
curve(cf.m[1] + cf.m[2]*x, add = TRUE, col = "red", lty = 1)

co <- format(c(coef(fit2), r2real), digits = 4)
text(3.5, 
     5.0,
     label = substitute(hat(y[i]) == b0 + b1*x[i] ~~~~ r^2 == r2,
                        list(b0 = co[1], b1 = co[2], r2 = co[3])))
box()
```

### 2.6 Fitting with mean and totals
```{r}
y1 <- c(5, 9, 10, 13, 13)
x1 <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
fit5 <- lm(y1 ~ x1)
summary(fit5)
anova(fit5)

y2 <- c(15, 27, 30, 39, 39)
x2 <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
fit6 <- lm(y2 ~ x2)
summary(fit6)
anova(fit6)
```

**Note:**

Both models yield the same regression equation form
When using totals, coefficients are multiplied by the number of replicates
Sums of squares also differ by a factor equal to the number of replicates

# Linear Second-Order Regression

## Example 3: Single values

A degree-p polynomial function can be represented as:
$$
y=\beta_0+\beta_1X^1+\beta_2X^2+...+\beta_pX^p+\varepsilon
$$
"According to the data provided below for variable X (Zn micro-nutrient dose in ppm) and variable Y (dry matter in g/plant), check—using a 5% probability level and a second-degree linear model—whether the relationship between variable X (independent) and Y (dependent) is significant.

```{r}
rm(list=ls()) 

x <- c(1.0, 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, 7.0, 8.5)
y <- c(20.3, 31.3, 34.6, 35.1, 30.2, 19.7)

ms <- data.frame(x, y)

plot(y ~ x, col = 4, pch = 19, data = ms,
     main = "Scatter plot: Dry matter vs Zinc dose",
     xlab = "Zinc dose (ppm)", ylab = "Dry matter (g/plant)")
```

As we can see the dots do not followed a linear distribution.

### 3. Model selection

### 3.1 Fit first-degree model
```{r}
fit1 <- lm(y ~ x)
summary(fit1)
anova(fit1)
```
**Only the intercept was significative.** Then, the first-degree model **does not** adequately explain the variability in $Y$. 

### 3.2 Fit second-order model

```{r}
fit3 <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2))
summary(fit3)
anova_fit3 <- anova(fit3)
print(anova_fit3, digits = 6)
```

However, when we check the significance for the second order analysis we verify 

### 3.2 Checking Assumptions
**Normality test**
```{r}
shapiro.test(fit3$res)
```

### 3.3 Computing R²

```{r}
R2<- summary(fit3)$r.squared
fit4 <- lm(y~factor(x))
R2max <- summary(fit4)$r.squared
Rreal <- R2/R2max
```

### 3.4 Adjusting a regressition plot
```{r}
plot(y ~ x, data = ms, pch = 16, col = "blue", xaxt = "n", 
     xlab = "Zinc dose (ppm)", ylab = "Dry matter (g/plant)", ylim = c(18, 40))
axis(1, xaxp = c(0, 10, 20))

cf.m4 <- coef(fit3)
curve(cf.m4[1] + cf.m4[2]*x + cf.m4[3]*x^2, add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

co <- format(c(coef(fit3), R2), digits = 4)
text(4.7, 27, label = substitute(hat(y[i])==b0+b1*x[i]+b2*x[i]^2~~~~R^2==r2,
                                 list(b0 = co[1], b1 = co[2], b2 = co[3], r2 = co[4])),
     bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

## With replicates
```{r}
# Clear environment
rm(list = ls())
ls()

# Load dataset
data <- read.table("DataReagente.txt", header = TRUE)
head(data)
attach(data)
```

Assumption checking (CRD)

```{r}

# Linear model treating x as a factor (for residual analysis)
fit1 <- lm(y ~ factor(x))
res <- fit1$residuals
res

# Normality test
shapiro.test(res)

# Homogeneity of variances
bartlett.test(res, x)
```

Fitting a quadratic regression model

```{r}
# Scatterplot
plot(x, y, pch = 19, col = "red", main = "Scatterplot: Response vs. Dose")

# Quadratic model
fit2 <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2))
summary(fit2)

# Coefficient of determination
R2 <- summary(fit2)$r.squared; R2
anova(fit2)
coef(fit2)
confint(fit2)
```


$𝑌= −0.2774 + 0.0323𝑋−0.000089𝑋^2$

Residual Sum of Squares = 3.6021 Includes both pure error and lack of fit

### Pure error and lack of fit analysis

```{r}
# Fit using x as a factor to capture pure error
fit3 <- lm(y ~ factor(x))
summary(fit3)
R2max <- summary(fit3)$r.squared; R2max
anova(fit3)

# Lack of fit test (comparing quadratic to full model)
anova(fit2, fit3)
anova(fit1, fit2)
```

**Results:**

- RSS (fit2): 3.6021 (27 df) 

- Pure Error: 2.9267 (20 df) 
- Lack of Fit: 0.6754 (7 df), F = 0.6594, p = 0.7031 → Not significant

```{r}
# Real R-squared
R2real <- R2 / R2max
R2real
```

Using ExpDes.pt for Analysis

```{r}
library(ExpDes.pt)

# Quantitative analysis
dic(x, y, quali = FALSE, mcomp = "tukey", sigT = 0.05, sigF = 0.06)

# Polynomial regression with known degrees of freedom and SS
dic <- lm(y ~ factor(x))
anova(dic)

reg.poly(y, x, 20, 2.9267, 9, 7.3430)
```

Plotting the Fitted Quadratic Model

```{r}
# Plot observed values
plot(y ~ x, data = data, pch = 16, col = "blue",
     xlab = "Dose X", ylab = "Response Y", ylim = c(0, 3),
     xaxt = "n", frame = FALSE)
axis(1, xaxp = c(50, 300, 10))  # custom ticks

# Add fitted curve
cf.m <- coef(fit2)
curve(cf.m[1] + cf.m[2]*x + cf.m[3]*I(x^2), add = TRUE, col = "red", lty = 1)

# Annotate with equation and R²
co <- format(c(coef(fit2), R2real), digits = 4)
text(160, 0.8, label = substitute(
  hat(y) == b0 + b1*x + b2*x^2 ~~~~ (R^2 == r2),
  list(b0 = co[1], b1 = co[2], b2 = co[3], r2 = co[4])))
```
